title: Only the injured spouse may thrash union
keywords: aggrieved or injured spouse legal personality

primary_topics: Figarido v. Figarido (Nov 5, 2024, per J. Ricardo R. Rosario, en banc, 9-4-1; released Feb 14, 2025) holding that only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse of either marriage may petition for nullity of a subsequent bigamous marriage

Facts: Maria Lina's 1989 first marriage to Ho Kar Wai (re-solemnized 1994); 2003 bigamous marriage to Edwin with two children; 2007 Hong Kong divorce; 2009 RTC Parañaque recognition; 2014 separation; 2017 petition denied; 2021 CA affirmed

Doctrinal basis: Section 2(a) of the 'Rule on Declaration of Absolute Nullity of Void Marriages' and its 'Rationale' -- only an aggrieved or injured spouse may file petitions for annulment of voidable marriages and declaration of absolute nullity of void marriages
CJ Gesmundo's concurrence anchoring the result in equity / unclean hands ('no man can be allowed to found a claim upon his own wrongdoing')

Lazaro-Javier dissent: the 'Rule' itself says 'solely by the husband or the wife'; the capacity requirement is in the 'Rationale,' not the 'Rule'; Maria Lina was in good faith based on local and Hong Kong legal advice
Zalameda dissent: the 'Rationale' is not mandatory and nothing in the Family Code supports the limitation; the State has no interest in preserving a bigamous marriage
Author's agreement with the majority: condemning the guilty party to perpetual incapacity to remarry is not too harsh a punishment for trifling with marriage as an inviolable social institution
Constitutional and international anchoring: UDHR, ICESCR, ICCPR, the Constitution, the Family Code, and SC decisions all recognize the integrity of the family and sanctity of marriage
sub_topics: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, and International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights all recognize integrity of family and sanctity of marriage

Citation: Figarido v. Figarido, Nov 5, 2024, per J. Ricardo R. Rosario, en banc, 9-4-1, released Feb 14, 2025

Facts timeline: 1989 first marriage (Maria Lina to Ho Kar Wai, Chinese national) → 1994 re-solemnized in Parañaque City → 2003 bigamous second marriage to Edwin (who knew of prior marriage) in Quezon City → two children born 2004 and 2007 → 2007 Hong Kong divorce decree obtained by Ho → 2009 RTC Parañaque recognition of divorce decree → 2014 separation; Maria Lina took custody; Edwin went overseas and was never heard from → 2017 Maria Lina filed for nullity of marriage to Edwin and for declaration of capacity to remarry → 2019 RTC denied → 2021 CA upheld
Section 2(a) of the 'Rule': 'a petition for (the) declaration of (the) absolute nullity of (a) void marriage may be filed solely by the husband or the wife'

'Rationale' for the 'Rule' (issued earlier by the Court): 'Only an aggrieved or injured spouse may file petitions for annulment of voidable marriages and declaration of absolute nullity of void marriages'
Maria Lina's argument: there is no injured party since her first husband had divorced her

Court's response: (1) denial is 'not a refusal to declare her bigamous marriage void, but rather a repudiation of Maria Lina's legal personality to file the said petition,' and (2) granting her petition would 'bastardize the institution of marriage to the prejudice of the State'
CJ Gesmundo's concurrence: 'one who seeks equity and justice must come to court with clean hands' and 'ex dolo malo non oritur actio -- no man can be allowed to found a claim upon his own wrongdoing'
J. Caguioa and J. Singh wrote enlightening concurrences

J. Lazaro-Javier dissent: 'Rule' itself says 'solely by the husband or the wife,' not 'only the aggrieved or injured spouse'; the capacity requirement is only in the 'Rationale,' not the 'Rule'; Maria Lina relied in good faith on a local attorney (seven-year absence allows remarriage) and a Hong Kong lawyer (two-year absence is a divorce ground)

Lazaro-Javier's Cariaga v. Republic argument (penned by J. Caguioa, First Division): unclean-hands doctrine does not apply to nullity of marriages without valid marriage license; by parity, should not apply to bigamous-marriage nullity

Caguioa's retort: 'Nowhere in Cariaga did the Court rule that the unclean hands doctrine applied or did not apply'; opposed Javier's reliance on US Court of Appeals decisions ('decisions of the US Supreme Court are merely persuasive, not binding, more so, the decision of a court of appeals')

J. Zalameda's dissent: 'Rationale' is not mandatory; nothing in the Family Code supports the Rationale's limitations; 'The State has no interest in preserving a bigamous marriage, and the Court should not refuse to declare this marriage void by primarily relying on technicalities'

Author's concurrence with majority: 'condemning the guilty party in a bigamous marriage to perpetual incapacity to remarry is not too harsh a punishment for trifling with marriage, an inviolable social institution that the Constitution protects and cherishes, and the Lord bound till death parts the couple'

stances.claim: Only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may petition to declare the nullity of a subsequent bigamous marriage — Maria Lina, having knowingly contracted the bigamous marriage with Edwin (who himself knew of her prior marriage), lacked the legal capacity to file the petition.
stances.evidence: Section 2(a) of the Rule; the Rationale; Court's denial as 'repudiation of Maria Lina's legal personality'

stances.claim: Granting Maria Lina's petition would 'bastardize the institution of marriage to the prejudice of the State' — even where the first husband has independently obtained a foreign divorce, the second-marriage spouse who knowingly contracted bigamy is not the proper party.
stances.rhetorical_move: state-interest-in-marriage articulation paired with equity refusal

stances.claim: The doctrine is anchored in the clean-hands maxim 'ex dolo malo non oritur actio — no man can be allowed to found a claim upon his own wrongdoing' — as CJ Gesmundo articulated in concurrence.
stances.evidence: CJ Gesmundo concurrence; classical equitable maxim

stances.claim: The dissents are stirring but unpersuasive. Lazaro-Javier's good-faith argument (reliance on local and Hong Kong legal advice) and her Cariaga parity argument cannot escape that the 'Rule' is read consistently with the 'Rationale'; and Caguioa correctly notes that decisions of the US Supreme Court are merely persuasive, much less those of US courts of appeals.
stances.evidence: Caguioa's retort quoted; 'Nowhere in Cariaga did the Court rule that the unclean hands doctrine applied or did not apply'

stances.claim: Author agrees with the majority: 'condemning the guilty party in a bigamous marriage to perpetual incapacity to remarry is not too harsh a punishment for trifling with marriage, an inviolable social institution that the Constitution protects and cherishes, and the Lord bound till death parts the couple.'

Maria Lina's good-faith defense, surfaced by Justice Lazaro-Javier in dissent: she had been advised by a local attorney that her first husband's seven-year absence allowed her to remarry, and by a Hong Kong lawyer that two-year absence is a divorce ground.

Zalameda's exclamation: 'The State has no interest in preserving a bigamous marriage, and the Court should not refuse to declare this marriage void by primarily relying on technicalities' — the column's most quotable dissent line.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes Figarido v. Figarido (Nov 5, 2024, per J. Ricardo R. Rosario, en banc, 9-4-1; released Feb 14, 2025) opening with the international-law anchoring: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights -- together with the Philippine Constitution, the Family Code, and the SC's decisions and rules -- recognize the integrity of the family and the sanctity of marriage; yet in 'flesh-and-bones cases' the best legal minds often disagree on how to interpret, apply, and enforce them. The facts: in 1989, Maria Lina married Ho Kar Wai (a Chinese national), re-solemnized in 1994; in 2003 she contracted a second (bigamous) marriage with Edwin (who knew of her prior marriage) and they had two children in 2004 and 2007; also in 2007, Ho obtained a Hong Kong divorce decree, which the RTC Parañaque recognized in 2009; in 2014, the couple separated and Edwin went overseas; in 2017, Maria Lina petitioned for nullity of her marriage to Edwin and for declaration of her capacity to remarry; the RTC denied (2019) and the CA upheld (2021). Affirming the CA, the SC held that only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may petition for nullity of the subsequent marriage; Maria Lina was not the aggrieved or injured spouse and thus lacked the legal capacity. The Court relied on Section 2(a) of the 'Rule on Declaration of Absolute Nullity of Void Marriages' ('may be filed solely by the husband or the wife') and its 'Rationale' ('Only an aggrieved or injured spouse may file petitions for annulment of voidable marriages and declaration of absolute nullity of void marriages'). Maria Lina argued there is no injured party since her first husband had divorced her; the Court replied that the denial is 'not a refusal to declare her bigamous marriage void, but rather a repudiation of Maria Lina's legal personality to file the said petition,' and that a grant would 'bastardize the institution of marriage to the prejudice of the State.' CJ Gesmundo, J. Caguioa, and J. Singh wrote enlightening concurrences; the CJ stressed 'one who seeks equity and justice must come to court with clean hands' and 'ex dolo malo non oritur actio -- no man can be allowed to found a claim upon his own wrongdoing.' Justices Lazaro-Javier and Zalameda dissented stirringly. Lazaro-Javier argued that the 'Rule' itself only says 'solely by the husband or the wife,' with the capacity requirement found only in the 'Rationale,' and that Maria Lina was in good faith based on local-attorney and Hong-Kong-lawyer advice; she invoked Cariaga v. Republic (penned by J. Caguioa, First Division) as parity for non-application of unclean hands. Caguioa retorted that 'Nowhere in Cariaga did the Court rule that the unclean hands doctrine applied or did not apply,' and opposed Javier's reliance on US Court of Appeals decisions ('decisions of the US Supreme Court are merely persuasive, not binding, more so, the decision of a court of appeals'). Zalameda insisted that the 'Rationale' is not mandatory and that nothing in the Family Code supports it: 'The State has no interest in preserving a bigamous marriage, and the Court should not refuse to declare this marriage void by primarily relying on technicalities.' The author agrees with the majority: 'condemning the guilty party in a bigamous marriage to perpetual incapacity to remarry is not too harsh a punishment for trifling with marriage, an inviolable social institution that the Constitution protects and cherishes, and the Lord bound till death parts the couple.'
